title: How Twinkies Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the Twinkie snack cake: its invention by James Dewar at Continental Bakeries (Hostess) in the 1930s, the banana cream original replaced by vanilla during WWII, the ingredient list and preservatives, a deep-fried Twinkie recipe, factory baking and cream injection, a nine-month Twinkie burial experiment by Oregon kids, pop culture references (Twinkie the Kid, Twinkie Gate, the Twinkie defense in the Dan White trial), Twinkies in the Millennium Time Capsule, a Rice University "TWINKIES" project testing water, gravity and sentience, and Twinkie-eating records. The episode closes with listener mail from Robin in Portland, Oregon, who was locked on an Amsterdam patio.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts joke around and tease Twinkie facts, including the banana cream original and the snack's size.

segments.title: Invention of the Twinkie
segments.summary: Continental Bakeries vice president James Dewar, idle strawberry shortcake machinery, and the billboard for Twinkletoe shoes that inspired the name.

segments.title: Banana cream filling and WWII
segments.summary: The original Twinkie had banana cream filling until wartime banana shortages led to vanilla; limited banana runs later boosted sales and banana flavor became permanent in 2007.

segments.title: Early Twinkie recipe and shelf life
segments.summary: The early Twinkie was made with eggs, milk and butter and had a shelf life of about two days, prompting Dewar's push for a longer-lasting version.

segments.title: Modern ingredients
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the roughly 39 ingredients, including corn syrup, bleached flour, monoglycerides, polysorbate 60, hydrogenated shortening, and artificial flavors made from petroleum.

segments.title: Twinkie recipes and fried Twinkies
segments.summary: Personal anecdotes about strawberry shortcake with Twinkies and Chuck's deep-fried Twinkie recipe sold at a beer festival.

segments.title: Factory baking and cream injection
segments.summary: How Twinkies are baked in metal pans at about 350 degrees for nine to twelve minutes, with the three holes in the bottom created by cream injectors, and sealed airtight in packaging.

segments.title: Preservation and the Oregon burial experiment
segments.summary: Sorbic acid is the only ingredient added specifically as a preservative; Hostess says shelf life is about 25 days, but two Oregon kids buried a Twinkie for nine months and reported it was fine.

segments.title: Twinkie the Kid and pop culture
segments.summary: Discussion of the Twinkie the Kid cowboy mascot, a fan's tattoo, and old Twinkie ads.

segments.title: Twinkie Gate and the Twinkie defense
segments.summary: George Draper's Minneapolis council campaign with Twinkies, coffee and Kool-Aid led to a bribery indictment; the Twinkie defense was used in the Dan White trial after the killings of Harvey Milk and Mayor George Moscone.

segments.title: Millennium Time Capsule
segments.summary: Bill Clinton selected a Twinkie for the Millennium Time Capsule alongside other items.

segments.title: Rice University TWINKIES project
segments.summary: Rice University students tested Twinkies in water (swelling and disintegration), dropping from a sixth-floor building (splitting but retaining structure), and a Turing test for sentience.

segments.title: Twinkie-eating records
segments.summary: Lewis Browning of Indiana has eaten a Twinkie a day since the 1950s and James Dewar reportedly ate about forty thousand. The hosts discuss whether Twinkies are healthy.

segments.title: Listener mail: locked out in Amsterdam
segments.summary: Robin of Portland, Oregon, locked herself out on an Amsterdam patio, was rescued after five hours, and says the podcast downloads helped her get through it.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts close the episode with a sign-off and a reminder about the listener mail address.
